video_title: Brent Johnson: Why This Bull Market Can Last Much Longer Than You Think
gist: Santiago Capital's Brent Johnson argues higher US rates and dollar stablecoins pull global capital into US assets at the expense of Europe and other countries, so the debt-driven system can run far longer than bears expect despite ending badly eventually. He details a US-centric portfolio: AI megacaps, short-duration credit, gold, grains, defense/reshoring private credit, stablecoin/tokenization names, and ~1% tail hedges, while growing constructive on Latin America.

themes.theme: Rate hikes as US capital magnet

insights.claim: Brent Johnson argues that the Fed's (Warsh-led) 25bp rate hike is not bearish for US equities because relatively higher US rates attract global capital that first parks in short-term dollar fixed income and then migrates into US risk assets, especially equities.
insights.speaker: Brent Johnson
insights.so_what: Don't reflexively sell US equities on modest Fed hikes; watch for foreign inflows rotating from T-bills into US stocks.
insights.quote: capital would migrate into US dollar uh risk assets most namely US equities

insights.claim: Johnson contends higher rates are stimulative within a range because the government pays more interest into the accounts of Treasury and T-bill holders, money that gets spent or reinvested — until rates rise so far (e.g., another 3-4%) that they 'hit the wall' and crash markets.
insights.speaker: Brent Johnson
insights.so_what: Treat incremental 25bp hikes as roughly neutral-to-supportive; the risk regime changes only with large cumulative hikes.
insights.quote: I have argued that higher rates are actually stimulative

insights.claim: A foreign investor earning 4-5% in short-term US fixed income while their local currency stays flat or falls versus the dollar earns a respectable return simply sitting in the global reserve currency.
insights.speaker: Brent Johnson
insights.so_what: Supports persistent foreign demand for front-end US paper and dollar strength versus other fiat currencies.

insights.claim: Johnson believes rising rates globally (Europe, Asia, Australia) will hurt the rest of the world sooner and more severely than the US, drawing even more capital to the US on a relative basis.
insights.speaker: Brent Johnson
insights.so_what: Favor US over international assets in a global rising-rate environment; expect relative stress abroad first.
insights.quote: when liquidity leaves, that causes problems

insights.claim: Johnson says the debt-driven system will end badly but 'imminent is not the same thing as inevitable'; investors expecting a quick collapse will be disappointed because authorities can keep kicking the can, with episodic volatility along the way.
insights.speaker: Brent Johnson
insights.so_what: Avoid being fully defensive waiting for the crisis; position for a long runway punctuated by volatility spikes.
insights.quote: imminent is not the same thing as inevitable

insights.claim: Johnson's 2018-19 call for a dollar 'super spike' within 4-5 years nearly played out in 2022, when aggressive hikes coincided with UK, European and Japanese sovereign-bond stress and an accelerating China real-estate collapse, but authorities ultimately kicked the can.
insights.speaker: Brent Johnson
insights.so_what: Shows the dollar-spike stress scenario remains latent; 2022 is the template for what a renewed squeeze looks like.

insights.claim: Johnson describes a vicious circle for Europe and a virtuous one for the US: capital flowing to the US creates conditions for more inflow, while capital leaving Europe creates conditions for more outflow, and the process is hard to reverse once started.
insights.speaker: Brent Johnson
insights.so_what: Structural underweight Europe vs US; reversal would require a major catalyst.
insights.quote: capital flowing to the United States creates the conditions under which more capital will flow to the United States

insights.claim: Europe's growth is already spoken for by social programs, interest on debt and NATO defense-spending mandates pushed by Trump, leaving little capital for productive enterprise, while higher European rates must be covered by growth or money printing.
insights.speaker: Brent Johnson
insights.so_what: Expect weak European productivity/returns and pressure toward monetization; bearish euro-area risk assets relative to US.

insights.claim: Johnson sees capital controls as potentially the only catalyst that could bring capital back to Europe.
insights.speaker: Brent Johnson
insights.so_what: Tail risk for foreign holders of European assets; capital-control headlines would be a key signal.
insights.quote: I don't see what the catalyst is going to be other than potentially capital controls to bring capital back to Europe

insights.claim: Norway's sovereign wealth fund, among the world's largest, has its biggest allocation to the US, illustrating how large global allocators choosing the US directly deprive Europe and China of inflows.
insights.speaker: Brent Johnson
insights.so_what: Monitor large sovereign/pension allocation shifts as a gauge of the US capital-magnet thesis.

insights.claim: Johnson argues that massive dollar-denominated debt in the eurodollar market forces the world to keep needing dollars to service interest and principal, regardless of whether they dislike Trump or America.
insights.speaker: Brent Johnson
insights.so_what: De-dollarization narratives understate structural dollar demand; fade 'dollar collapse' trades.
insights.quote: what we want and what we have to do are two different things

insights.claim: After the US and allies froze roughly $300-400 billion of Russian reserves in 2022, the dollar index rose from about 98 to 114 within six months rather than falling, because energy and food priced in dollars spiked.
insights.speaker: Brent Johnson
insights.so_what: Geopolitical shocks that raise commodity prices tend to strengthen, not weaken, the dollar.
insights.quote: the dollar index went from like 98 to 114 in six months

insights.claim: Johnson says any non-dollar reserve system (e.g., a gold- or Bitcoin-backed basket stablecoin) faces a currency-mismatch problem because most global institutions have dollar liabilities, so holding non-dollar reserves adds risk most will avoid.
insights.speaker: Brent Johnson
insights.so_what: Raises the bar for BRICS or basket-currency alternatives to dent dollar dominance.

insights.claim: Johnson views the GENIUS Act as the US state co-opting a private, system-escaping innovation (stablecoins) to extend dollar control, succeeding largely because the eurodollar system already created structural global dollar dependence.
insights.speaker: Brent Johnson
insights.so_what: US policy is a tailwind for dollar stablecoin issuers and infrastructure.
insights.quote: How can we co-opt this for our own benefit?

insights.claim: About 99% of all stablecoins in existence are US-dollar stablecoins, which Johnson says reflects global demand for dollars rather than issuers forcing the dollar on the world.
insights.speaker: Brent Johnson
insights.so_what: Euro/gold stablecoins are niche; dollar stablecoin rails dominate.
insights.quote: 99% of all stable coins in existence are US dollar stable coins

insights.claim: Johnson argues dollar stablecoins strip monetary sovereignty from foreign governments as citizens prefer dollar balances to local currency, a stealthy non-military US 'invasion' that leaves other countries choosing between losing competition with their own stablecoins or stifling growth via capital controls.
insights.speaker: Brent Johnson
insights.so_what: Watch for foreign regulatory backlash against USD stablecoins; EM currencies face added pressure from dollarization.
insights.quote: a surreptitious stealthy way for the US to kind of invade

insights.claim: Over the last 12 months central banks and monetary authorities worldwide have increasingly voiced concern about US-dollar stablecoins' impact on their local economies, a pattern Johnson says was absent 2-3 years ago.
insights.speaker: Brent Johnson
insights.so_what: Regulatory headline risk outside the US is rising; a sign the dollarization effect is real.

insights.claim: Johnson expects 24-hour tokenized trading to favor the US because global liquidity will prefer trading the Nasdaq or S&P 500 around the clock over smaller, less liquid markets such as Thailand or South Africa.
insights.speaker: Brent Johnson
insights.so_what: Tokenization likely deepens US market liquidity premium at the expense of smaller exchanges.
insights.quote: why on earth are you going to move your liquidity to trade Thailand when the United States is asleep?

insights.claim: The host, who runs a Netherlands-based crypto and commodities fund, finds liquidity so poor when trading against the euro that risk rises sharply versus trading against the US dollar.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: Practitioner evidence that non-dollar crypto liquidity remains thin.

insights.claim: Citing Mike Green, Johnson argues the rise of market-cap-weighted passive funds makes markets narrative-driven: algorithms mechanically buy what rises, exaggerating moves in both directions until something dramatic turns the ship, after which reversals can be just as fast.
insights.speaker: Brent Johnson
insights.so_what: Expect momentum extremes and sharp reversals; keep dry powder to exploit narrative breaks.
insights.quote: The machines are doing it.

insights.claim: Johnson holds short-term T-bills/cash as tactical dry powder specifically to buy dislocations when narratives break, calling this the best way for value investors to benefit in current markets.
insights.speaker: Brent Johnson
insights.so_what: Paying 4-5% to wait makes holding optionality cheap.

insights.claim: Johnson's tactical portfolio seeks extremes: buying puts or shorting when assets are extremely expensive and going long when they are severely beaten down.
insights.speaker: Brent Johnson
insights.so_what: A reusable approach for a narrative-driven market: fade extremes with a liquid sleeve.

insights.claim: Johnson first bought gold for clients in 2006 around $700, added near $600 during the GFC, then endured roughly seven to eight years around $1,100-1,200 before valuations paid off well, illustrating the patience value investing requires.
insights.speaker: Brent Johnson
insights.so_what: Long-dated value positions should be sized as a portion of the portfolio you can hold through years of no return.

insights.claim: Johnson calls the current period the most challenging in his 26 years of managing money and says he prepares for scenarios rather than predicting, because sitting out waiting for the inevitable crisis risks missing years of opportunity.
insights.speaker: Brent Johnson
insights.so_what: Scenario-based, barbelled positioning beats binary crisis bets.
insights.quote: this is probably the most challenging period of time in managing money

insights.claim: Johnson holds Nvidia, Taiwan Semiconductor, Google and Meta despite believing their valuations are 'kind of ridiculous', hedging that risk with other portfolio sleeves designed to gain in a big dislocation.
insights.speaker: Brent Johnson
insights.so_what: Own AI leaders but pair them with explicit drawdown hedges.
insights.quote: Yeah, I I kind of do think they're ridiculous

insights.claim: Johnson argues the arc of history has swung toward deglobalization, where national security trumps efficiency and locally sourced products trump price, as the US-China power competition reshapes supply chains.
insights.speaker: Brent Johnson
insights.so_what: Favor reshoring, friend-shoring and security-linked industries over pure cost-efficiency plays.
insights.quote: national security now trumps efficiency

insights.claim: Johnson treats AI data centers and the AI supply chain as a national-security imperative, echoing Palantir CEO Alex Karp's line that in AI there is first place and then extinction.
insights.speaker: Brent Johnson
insights.so_what: State backing reduces downside for strategic AI infrastructure even as valuation risk stays high.

insights.claim: Johnson expects AI to play out like the dot-com boom: many companies go bankrupt and valuations evaporate, but a handful become dominant for 5-15 years, as Amazon did for holders who endured the early-2000s losses.
insights.speaker: Brent Johnson
insights.so_what: Expect a shakeout; position in likely survivors and be prepared for large interim drawdowns.

insights.claim: Johnson sees Central and South America as possibly the biggest winners of US-China decoupling as manufacturing migrates from Asia, and says he is becoming increasingly constructive and starting small positions for a 10-20 year horizon.
insights.speaker: Brent Johnson
insights.so_what: Early-stage long-term allocation idea: Latin American nearshoring beneficiaries.
insights.quote: I think that timing might be now

insights.claim: Johnson's portfolios are predominantly US, with large-cap US equities, little international equity exposure on a risk-reward basis, and US credit preferred over emerging-market or foreign credit.
insights.speaker: Brent Johnson
insights.so_what: Concrete model allocation: US-centric with global revenue exposure via US multinationals.

insights.claim: Johnson keeps fixed income at two years' maturity or less because he would not be surprised if rates stay high or go higher, avoiding duration risk while earning 4-5%.
insights.speaker: Brent Johnson
insights.so_what: Stay short duration; avoid long bonds in a higher-for-longer world.

insights.claim: Johnson thinks private credit is broadly in a bubble but is allocating to private credit for companies focused on US national defense and reshoring supply chains, expecting one of the largest capital waves anyone has seen over the next 5-10 years.
insights.speaker: Brent Johnson
insights.so_what: Be selective in private credit; defense and reshoring borrowers may be the exception to the bubble.
insights.quote: We think private credit is in many ways in a bubble

insights.claim: Johnson expresses US national defense exposure through a combination of private credit and stock options, and holds grains such as corn and wheat expecting potential upside, alongside a permanent strategic gold allocation.
insights.speaker: Brent Johnson
insights.so_what: Commodities (precious metals and grains) are an increasing allocation for inflation scenarios.

insights.claim: Johnson allocates typically under 2%, usually about 1%, of portfolios to tail-risk hedges designed to become a large part of the portfolio in a 2008- or 2020-type event.
insights.speaker: Brent Johnson
insights.so_what: Small, persistent convexity sleeve as insurance against crash scenarios.

insights.claim: Johnson is invested in tokenization and stablecoin infrastructure, including Circle, Figure and Ethereum, plus smaller stablecoin-related companies, as a diversified basket bet that blockchain-based digital assets are the future.
insights.speaker: Brent Johnson
insights.so_what: Basket approach to the stablecoin/tokenization theme rather than picking one winner.
insights.quote: we think tokenization is here to stay

insights.claim: Johnson describes a K-shaped economy where fiat debasement, which he expects to increase as governments finance their debts, widens the gap between the top and bottom, which will eventually end badly but not necessarily soon.
insights.speaker: Brent Johnson
insights.so_what: Asset owners benefit from debasement; position in real and risk assets rather than cash long term.
insights.quote: the top half keeps getting higher and the lower half keeps going lower

insights.claim: Johnson argues Western governments are becoming more centrally planned, like China and Russia, and that greater state control and financial repression can still 'work' for long periods, as China's 25-30 year rise and Russia's recovery under Putin show.
insights.speaker: Brent Johnson
insights.so_what: Don't exit Western markets solely because policy is becoming less free; state-directed economies can still produce returns.
insights.quote: just because things don't work the way we would like doesn't mean they won't work
